L'AQUILA, Italy (CNN) -- The youngest hadn't lived half a year. The oldest had lived nearly a hundred. A rescue worker Friday kisses the coffin of a child killed by this week's earthquake in central Italy. The official government list of victims from this week's earthquake in central Italy reached 287 on Friday, as Italians held a mass state funeral to lay the victims to rest. They included Antonio Loavan Ghiroceanu, who was born December 11. He would have been  6 months old on Saturday. The oldest-known victim of the quake was Evandro Testa, 96, who was born in 1913. More than 200 caskets were lined up at the funeral, draped with flowers. At least one small white coffin belonging to a child sat atop a larger coffin, a baby's pastel outfit hanging off the side. The funeral was being held outside a hangar in Coppito, a town adjacent to the earthquake's epicenter of L'Aquila. Officials elected to hold the Mass in the open air to avoid the risk of injury from falling debris. Aftershocks continue to shake the region more than four days after the earthquake, and some were even felt during Friday's funeral. All of the area's cardinals and bishops, along with 100 priests, attended the special funeral Mass. Italian Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi was also there, greeting and embracing some of the thousands of mourners before the service. Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone presided over the Mass as an envoy from Pope Benedict XVI, who plans to visit the region after Easter.  Watch Italy bury its dead » . Bertone said the funeral was a "precious moment" to understand the meaning of life and death. "Everything can stop in a second -- projects, plans -- everything finishes. All that remains is love," he said. Watch more on funeral . Mourners, who were transported to the funeral on buses, dabbed their eyes and noses. Some stared at the ground or held each other. Few appeared focused on anything but remembering the victims. "I feel rebirth in the heart, because below that rubble there is a will to rebuild, to start again, to plan and to dream," Bertone said, offering a message of hope. The towns of L'Aquila and the surrounding region, he said, "will come back stronger, will have more courage and give life to these places with that power and strength and dignity of the soul that distinguishes them." As well as sending Bertone to deliver his message, the pope sent holy oils to L'Aquila and a chalice with which to take Communion. Archbishop Giuseppe Molinari of L'Aquila also planned to deliver a message. The 6.3-magnitude quake Monday morning left about 30,000 people without their homes. Almost 20,000 of them are braving chilly nights in tents while about 11,000 others are staying in hotels, said Agostino Miozzo, a spokesman for the Italian Civil Protection Agency. Watch more on the aftermath . Recovering from such losses and rebuilding the city of L'Aquila will take several years, according to Miozzo. The medieval city is about 120 km (75 miles) northeast of Rome. Berlusconi has said rebuilding will cost several billion euros. Aftershocks have heightened anxiety in the area -- including a moderate 5.6 magnitude tremor that struck the area Tuesday. "The mood is a little bit afraid," said Marco Volponi of the Civil Protection agency. He was working in a tent camp, housing people whose homes were inhabitable. In the nearby village of Onna, 40 people -- more than one out of every eight residents in the town of 300 -- were killed in the earthquake. On some streets, every single home was destroyed. Anna Rita Difilice lost her son, Fabio, 20, to the quake -- the deadliest to strike Italy in decades and the first major quake in the country in seven years. She said she doesn't know what comes next for her. Her village has become populated with tents, fold-up beds and feeding stations handing out food, water and other supplies for survivors. But she said she knew one thing: she's not going anywhere. "My son died here," she said. "There is no way I'm leaving this town -- not ever."

outputs.L1:
**L’AQUILA, Italy (CNN) —** The youngest had not lived even half a year; the oldest had lived nearly a century.

On Friday, a rescue worker kissed the coffin of a child killed in this week’s earthquake in central Italy.

The Italian government’s official list of victims reached 287 on Friday, as the nation held a state funeral Mass to lay the dead to rest.

Among the victims was Antonio Loavan Ghiroceanu, born on December 11, who would have been 6 months old on Saturday. The oldest known victim was Evandro Testa, 96, who was born in 1913.

More than 200 caskets, draped with flowers, were arranged at the funeral. At least one small white coffin belonging to a child rested atop a larger coffin, with a baby’s pastel outfit hanging over the side.

The funeral was held outside a hangar in Coppito, a town adjacent to the earthquake’s epicenter in L’Aquila. Officials chose to celebrate the Mass in the open air to avoid the danger of falling debris.

Aftershocks continued to shake the region more than four days after the earthquake, and some were felt during Friday’s funeral.

All of the area’s cardinals and bishops attended the special funeral Mass, along with 100 priests. Italian Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi was also present, greeting and embracing some of the thousands of mourners before the service.

Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone presided over the Mass as an envoy of Pope Benedict XVI, who plans to visit the region after Easter.

*Watch Italy bury its dead »*

Bertone described the funeral as a “precious moment” in which to understand the meaning of life and death.

“Everything can stop in a second — projects, plans — everything finishes. All that remains is love,” he said.

*Watch more on the funeral.*

Mourners, who were transported to the service by bus, dabbed their eyes and noses. Some stared at the ground; others held one another. Few appeared focused on anything other than remembering the victims.

“I feel rebirth in the heart, because below that rubble there is a will to rebuild, to start again, to plan and to dream,” Bertone said, offering a message of hope.

The towns of L’Aquila and the surrounding region, he said, “will come back stronger, will have more courage and give life to these places with that power and strength and dignity of the soul that distinguishes them.”

In addition to sending Bertone to deliver his message, the pope sent holy oils to L’Aquila and a chalice for Communion. Archbishop Giuseppe Molinari of L’Aquila also planned to deliver a message.

Monday morning’s 6.3-magnitude earthquake left approximately 30,000 people without homes. Nearly 20,000 were enduring chilly nights in tents, while about 11,000 others were staying in hotels, according to Agostino Miozzo, a spokesman for the Italian Civil Protection Agency.

*Watch more on the aftermath.*

Recovering from such losses and rebuilding L’Aquila will take several years, Miozzo said. The medieval city lies about 120 kilometers (75 miles) northeast of Rome. Berlusconi has said the reconstruction will cost several billion euros.

Aftershocks have heightened anxiety throughout the area, including a moderate 5.6-magnitude tremor that struck on Tuesday.

“The mood is a little bit afraid,” said Marco Volponi of the Civil Protection Agency. He was working at a tent camp housing people whose homes were uninhabitable.

In the nearby village of Onna, 40 people — more than one in every eight residents of the town of 300 — were killed in the earthquake. On some streets, every home was destroyed.

Anna Rita Difilice lost her 20-year-old son, Fabio, in the quake — the deadliest to strike Italy in decades and the country’s first major earthquake in seven years. She said she did not know what would come next for her.

Her village had become filled with tents, folding beds, and feeding stations distributing food, water, and other supplies to survivors. But she said she knew one thing: she was not going anywhere.

“My son died here,” she said. “There is no way I’m leaving this town — not ever.”

**Mourners bury L’Aquila’s dead as survivors face years of rebuilding**

**L’AQUILA, Italy, April 10, 2009** — Rows of polished wooden coffins filled the parade ground of a police training academy Friday as thousands of mourners gathered for a state funeral honoring victims of the 6.3-magnitude earthquake that devastated this medieval city and surrounding mountain towns.

Relatives leaned over the coffins, touching photographs, flowers and handwritten notes. Some knelt in prayer; others stood in silence, wrapped in blankets against the morning cold. Small white caskets belonging to children lay among those of parents, grandparents and students killed when homes and apartment buildings collapsed before dawn Monday.

The Mass, held under an open-sided canopy because many churches remain unsafe, brought together grieving families, rescue workers and Italy’s political leadership. Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone, representing Pope Benedict XVI, led the Catholic service. An imam later offered prayers for Muslim victims, reflecting the diverse community caught in the disaster.

More than 200 coffins were present at the ceremony. The confirmed death toll had risen to about 290, with officials warning that it could increase as crews continued searching unstable buildings and reconciling lists of missing residents.

Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi and President Giorgio Napolitano attended amid tight security. But for many families, the ceremony was less a national event than an intensely private farewell.

“I have lost everything,” one mourner said as relatives supported her near a coffin covered with flowers. Around her, the names and ages of the dead revealed the earthquake’s reach: university students trapped in dormitories, entire families buried in apartment blocks and elderly residents killed in homes that had stood for generations.

Church bells sounded across the region at the start of the funeral. Shops closed, flags flew at half-staff and the country observed a day of mourning.

### Tens of thousands without homes

Beyond the funeral ground, the emergency was entering a difficult new phase. Tens of thousands of people had been driven from their homes, either because the buildings were destroyed or because aftershocks made it too dangerous to return.

Tent camps spread across sports fields and open land around L’Aquila. Residents slept on narrow cots beneath canvas, lining up for hot meals, bottled water, medical care and information about missing relatives. Others were moved to hotels along the Adriatic coast, sometimes more than an hour away.

Officials said sheltering people in hotels would provide greater comfort and safety, especially for families with young children and older residents. But the transfers also threatened to scatter communities already traumatized by the disaster.

One mother living with her children in a temporary camp refused to leave L’Aquila for accommodation on the coast. Her home was unsafe, but she said she would remain near the city rather than abandon the place where her family had lived and where friends and relatives were still searching, grieving and trying to recover belongings.

Her refusal reflected a growing dilemma among survivors: whether to accept safer housing far away or remain close to damaged homes, schools and neighborhoods with no clear timetable for returning.

For many residents, leaving even temporarily felt like a second loss.

### Aftershocks deepen fear

Repeated aftershocks continued to shake the region, sending frightened residents rushing from tents and rescue workers away from weakened walls. Each tremor raised fears that more of L’Aquila’s historic center could collapse.

Authorities maintained restrictions around the most heavily damaged areas. Residents were allowed into some buildings only briefly and, in many cases, only when accompanied by firefighters. They emerged carrying documents, clothing, family photographs and bags of medicine.

The earthquake caused extensive damage to apartment blocks, government buildings, churches and monuments. Parts of L’Aquila’s historic center — known for stone palaces, narrow streets and centuries-old churches — were sealed off because falling masonry made them too dangerous to enter.

Prosecutors also began examining why some relatively modern buildings collapsed while older structures nearby remained standing. Questions centered on construction standards, materials and whether anti-seismic rules had been properly enforced.

### Reconstruction could cost billions

The government pledged to rebuild L’Aquila and the surrounding communities, but early estimates suggested the work would cost many billions of euros. Initial projections placed the total burden at roughly €12 billion, although officials cautioned that a reliable figure would not be possible until engineers completed a building-by-building assessment.

The expense will extend far beyond replacing homes. Roads, schools, hospitals, public offices, university facilities and water and power systems must be repaired. Restoring the city’s historic churches and monuments could take years and require specialized work.

The immediate priority, officials said, was to inspect homes and determine which residents could safely return. Temporary housing would then be needed for those whose buildings were destroyed or required extensive repairs.

Berlusconi promised that reconstruction would begin quickly and that communities would not be abandoned. Survivors, however, voiced concern that emergency attention could fade once the funerals ended and television crews left.

The challenge is not only financial. Engineers must rebuild in a region that remains vulnerable to earthquakes, while preserving the character of towns whose identities are tied to ancient stone buildings and tightly packed historic centers.

As the funeral concluded, relatives followed the coffins away for burial in cemeteries across the region. Rescue crews returned to the ruins, and displaced families went back to tents, hotels and cars.

For L’Aquila, the day marked neither an end to the search nor the beginning of normal life. It was a pause — a collective farewell before the long work of accounting for the missing, housing the survivors and rebuilding a city whose residents, like the mother who refused to leave, remain determined not to surrender their home.

# Italy mourns L’Aquila earthquake victims at mass state funeral

**COPPITO, Italy — April 10, 2009** — Rows of polished wooden coffins filled the parade ground of a police academy outside L’Aquila on Friday as Italy held a state funeral for victims of the devastating earthquake that struck the central Abruzzo region four days earlier.

Relatives leaned over caskets, touching photographs and handwritten notes taped to the wood. Some placed flowers beside the coffins; others rested their heads against them and wept. Several small white coffins, including those of children, stood among the larger ones. In one particularly painful image, a baby’s coffin was placed on top of the casket of the child’s mother.

More than 200 coffins were brought to the ceremony at the Guardia di Finanza police academy in Coppito. Thousands of mourners crowded behind barriers and watched from large screens, while firefighters, soldiers, rescue workers and volunteers stood in formation nearby.

Church bells rang across Italy, flags flew at half-staff and the country observed a national day of mourning. Shops and government offices closed in parts of the region, and many television and radio stations suspended their normal programming.

The funeral took place on Good Friday, when the Roman Catholic Church ordinarily does not celebrate funeral Masses. The Vatican granted a special dispensation because of the scale of the disaster.

Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone, the Vatican secretary of state and Pope Benedict XVI’s representative, presided over the service. Italian President Giorgio Napolitano and Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi were among the officials in attendance.

In a message read at the ceremony, Benedict expressed his sorrow and spiritual closeness to the bereaved. The pope said he hoped those who had lost family members, homes and livelihoods would find consolation amid “such great suffering.”

The Catholic service was followed by Islamic prayers for Muslim victims of the earthquake. An imam stood before several coffins and recited verses from the Quran as Catholic clergy and Italian officials remained in place—an uncommon and striking interfaith moment at a national ceremony in overwhelmingly Roman Catholic Italy.

## “Why them and not me?”

The funeral ground was silent except for prayers, sobbing and the occasional cry of a relative calling the name of someone who had died. Many mourners wore dark glasses against the bright spring sun; others carried portraits of the victims as they had been before the earthquake—at weddings, graduations or family gatherings.

When the names of the dead were read, grief repeatedly broke through the solemn order of the ceremony. Family members clung to one another. Rescue workers who had spent days digging through collapsed buildings wiped their eyes.

As the service ended, mourners applauded—a traditional Italian gesture of respect—as some coffins were carried away. The applause grew louder for firefighters and civil protection teams, many of whom had worked with little sleep since the earthquake struck.

Survivors spoke of guilt as well as grief. The question heard repeatedly in the camps and outside the funeral was simple: Why did one building collapse while the one beside it remained standing? Why did one family escape while another was buried?

Residents described being awakened by violent shaking at 3:32 a.m. Monday. Walls cracked, floors shifted and entire sections of apartment buildings collapsed within seconds. People fled into streets filled with dust, broken glass and falling masonry, many dressed only in nightclothes.

In L’Aquila’s historic center, centuries-old churches, stone houses and government buildings were badly damaged. Streets were blocked by rubble, and rescue workers searched cavities in collapsed buildings while aftershocks sent fresh debris tumbling from weakened walls.

## Death toll continued to rise

At the time of the funeral, Italian authorities put the death toll at about 289, with roughly 1,500 people injured. More bodies were still being recovered, and some of the critically injured remained in hospitals across central Italy.

The final toll was later revised to **309 dead**.

Among the victims were children, university students, elderly residents, immigrants and entire families. L’Aquila’s large student population was hit particularly hard when apartment blocks and a student residence collapsed.

The magnitude-6.3 earthquake, according to the U.S. Geological Survey, was centered near L’Aquila, about 95 kilometers—roughly 60 miles—northeast of Rome. Italian seismologists measured it at magnitude 5.8 using a different scale and methodology.

The quake was felt in Rome and across much of central Italy. It was followed by hundreds of aftershocks, several strong enough to force rescue workers to retreat temporarily from unstable ruins.

## Tens of thousands without homes

Beyond the funeral, the humanitarian emergency was still unfolding.

Tens of thousands of people had been driven from their homes. Italian authorities estimated that as many as 65,000 residents were displaced, although the number staying in organized camps varied as people moved among tents, hotels, relatives’ homes and temporary shelters.

Large tent cities appeared on football fields, parking lots and open ground around L’Aquila. Blue government-issued tents stood in long rows, with portable toilets, field kitchens and medical stations set up nearby.

Volunteers distributed bottled water, hot meals, blankets, clothing and basic medicines. Military personnel helped control access to damaged districts, while engineers inspected buildings to determine whether residents could safely return.

For many, the answer was no.

Families who had escaped with only a few possessions waited for information about their homes. Some stood near police checkpoints asking to be allowed back inside long enough to retrieve documents, medication or photographs. Authorities often refused because of the risk of collapse.

Nighttime temperatures fell sharply, and rain made conditions in some camps more difficult. Survivors complained of cold, crowding, limited privacy and uncertainty over how long they would remain under canvas. Parents tried to calm children frightened by every vibration, slamming door or passing truck.

Aftershocks were especially terrifying. Each tremor sent people running from tents or gathering in open spaces, even when there were no buildings nearby that could fall.

Civil protection officials said food and water supplies were generally adequate, but the challenge was enormous: registering displaced families, reuniting relatives, caring for the elderly and disabled, treating trauma and finding longer-term housing before temporary camps became permanent.

Berlusconi promised that the government would rebuild L’Aquila and surrounding towns. He said survivors would not be abandoned, though many residents expressed concern about how quickly reconstruction could begin and whether the medieval city center could ever be restored.

## Questions over construction and warnings

Even as rescuers searched for survivors, anger grew over the collapse of relatively modern buildings.

Prosecutors opened an investigation into whether poor construction, substandard materials or failures to follow anti-seismic regulations contributed to the death toll. Residents asked why some reinforced-concrete buildings had crumbled in an area long known to be vulnerable to earthquakes.

Particular attention focused on structures that should have offered protection, including a hospital wing, student housing and apartment buildings.

There was also controversy over a series of smaller tremors that had shaken the region for months. Some residents said they had become increasingly alarmed before the main quake. Officials and scientists countered that earthquakes cannot be predicted with enough precision to justify evacuating an entire city.

At the funeral, however, those disputes briefly gave way to collective mourning.

Cardinal Bertone urged Italians not to allow death and destruction to erase solidarity. Clergy spoke of the rescue workers who had crawled through unstable ruins, neighbors who had pulled one another from rubble and volunteers who had arrived from across the country.

The scale of the loss was visible in the coffins stretching across the academy grounds.

Some bore only a nameplate and flowers. Others were covered with football scarves, photographs, children’s drawings or messages from friends. Relatives remained beside them until officials began preparing to move the caskets to cemeteries across Abruzzo and other parts of Italy.

Outside the academy, survivors returned to tent camps, damaged villages and an uncertain future. Rescue crews went back to the ruins, though hopes of finding more people alive were fading.

For L’Aquila, the funeral marked neither the end of the emergency nor the beginning of normal life. It was a pause—a few hours in which a shattered city and a grieving country stood together before confronting the longer tasks of burying the dead, sheltering the living and rebuilding what the earthquake had destroyed.
